subject: history

moments.title: Trinity test
moments.body: 16 July 1945: the first nuclear weapon detonates in the New Mexico desert. Yield around 22 kilotons. Oppenheimer later recalls thinking of the Bhagavad Gita: 'Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.' The Manhattan Project had cost $2 billion (around $30 billion today) and employed 130,000 people.
moments.takeaway: Truman receives word at Potsdam. He authorises use against Japan without further deliberation.

moments.title: Hiroshima and Nagasaki
moments.body: 6 August 1945: 'Little Boy' uranium bomb destroys Hiroshima — around 80,000 killed instantly, perhaps 140,000 by year end. 9 August: 'Fat Man' plutonium bomb destroys Nagasaki — around 40,000 instant, 70,000 by year end. Japan surrenders 15 August.

quote.text: We have used it in order to shorten the agony of war.

moments.takeaway: The USSR declared war on Japan on 8 August. Whether the Soviet declaration or the bombs were decisive for Japan's surrender is contested by historians (Tsuyoshi Hasegawa, 2005).

moments.title: Soviet bomb and thermonuclear weapons
moments.body: August 1949: USSR tests its first bomb (RDS-1), helped by espionage (Klaus Fuchs). 1952: US tests the first thermonuclear (Ivy Mike, 10.4 megatons). 1953: USSR follows. Stockpiles peak around 70,000 warheads in the mid-1980s.
moments.takeaway: Mutual Assured Destruction (MAD) became the framework. Treaty regimes (PTBT 1963, NPT 1968, SALT, START) constrained the arms race.

now.title: The bomb in the modern world
now.body: Nine nuclear-armed states: US, Russia, UK, France, China, India, Pakistan, Israel (undeclared), North Korea. The Russia-Ukraine war (since 2022) has reintroduced explicit nuclear threats into European politics. The Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (2017, in force 2021) is opposed by all nuclear states.
now.open_questions: Were the bombings necessary? Gar Alperovitz argued they were unnecessary given Soviet entry; others (Richard Frank) argue the Japanese government was not poised to surrender without them. The moral question and the historical question are not the same.

reflection: The atomic bombs ended one war and inaugurated a new logic of international security. 80 years later, the weapons still exist, the deterrent argument still holds, and the moral question has not been closed.
